paper.title: Original demonstration — Academic Reading
paper.instructions:
This is a short demonstration test, not a real IELTS paper. It exists to show every question type the app supports.

You should answer all 12 questions. Read the instructions for each set carefully and observe any word limit given.

You can change your answers at any time before the test ends.

parts.heading: Reading Passage 1
parts.instructions: You should spend about 15 minutes on Questions 1–12, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.

passage.title: The Lighthouse Keepers
passage.subtitle: For three centuries a scattered profession kept the coastlines lit. Then, within a single generation, it disappeared almost entirely.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The job of the lighthouse keeper was, for most of its history, defined less by heroism than by repetition. A keeper trimmed wicks, polished lenses, wound the clockwork that turned the light, and recorded the weather in a logbook at fixed hours. The work was exacting rather than difficult, and its central demand was consistency: a light that failed for even an hour could undo the reputation of a station built over decades.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Isolation shaped the profession more than any other factor. Offshore towers, known in the service as rock stations, might be supplied only every few weeks, and in poor weather a relief boat could be delayed for months. Keepers at such postings worked in teams of three, an arrangement adopted after an incident in which a keeper died and his sole companion, fearing an accusation of murder, kept the body on the gallery until the relief arrived. Three men meant that no one was ever alone with a corpse, or with a decision.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Onshore stations were a different life entirely. Families lived alongside the keeper, children walked to village schools, and gardens were cultivated in the lee of the tower. The service encouraged this: a keeper with a household nearby was thought less likely to abandon a difficult posting. Pay was modest but the accommodation was free, and the position carried a respectability out of proportion to its salary.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Technology eroded the profession gradually and then all at once. Clockwork mechanisms gave way to electric motors, oil lamps to sealed-beam bulbs, and manual weather observation to automatic instruments. Each change removed a task. By the middle of the twentieth century a keeper's duties had contracted to little more than supervision, and supervision is precisely what a telemetry link can provide from a distance.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The final wave of automation was swift. Britain removed its last resident keepers in 1998; Canada, unusually, retained staffed stations on parts of its western coast into the present century, arguing that keepers provided weather reports and rescue assistance that machines could not. That argument has never been fully settled. Automated lights are cheaper and, by most measures, no less reliable, but they cannot see a small boat in trouble and report it.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What has survived is the architecture. Towers that were built to be functional are now protected as heritage, and a surprising number have been converted into accommodation for visitors who pay for precisely the isolation that keepers once endured as a condition of employment. The lens rooms, stripped of their original optics, are the most photographed rooms in the buildings.

paragraphs.text: The community seed library opened in March. Its seed drawers are kept in the public library. Green packets contain vegetables, while blue packets contain flowers. Visitors may borrow three packets at a time. Members record the sowing date in a shared notebook. Volunteers teach monthly workshops in the annex. Beans have proved the most popular crop. Gardeners use netting to protect young plants from birds and wood to make reusable labels. Staff check stock weekly. After the harvest, members return seeds from healthy plants. Membership is free and spring is the busiest season.

groups.limit: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER

paragraphs.text: The coastal research station opened in 2014. Its outer walls are timber. Large windows face south. Solar panels generate most of the electricity, and batteries store the surplus. Six permanent researchers live on site. Each morning they monitor seabirds on the cliffs. Sensors measure water temperature and staff collect water samples daily. A ferry carries these samples to the mainland. The laboratory is kept at a constant temperature. Visiting school groups may use microscopes to examine specimens. November is reserved for maintenance, so the station is closed to visitors. Climate is the principal research topic.

groups.limit: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER
